eyebrow: KEY STAGE 3 HISTORY • YEAR 9 ENQUIRY CHRONOLOGY • 21 MILESTONES

eras.title: Part 1: Ideological Roots, Grand Alliance Breakdown & Divided Europe (1917–1949)
Part 2: Korean War, H-Bombs, Space Race & Building the Berlin Wall (1949–1961)
Part 3: Nuclear Brinkmanship in Cuba, Vietnam & Global Proxy Toll (1962–1975)
Part 4: Afghanistan, Gorbachev, Fall of the Berlin Wall & Soviet Collapse (1979–1991)

milestones.title: Capitalism vs Communism & Pre-1945 Mutual Betrayals
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rival ideas turn the USA and USSR into enemies after 1945?
milestones.imageCaption: Joseph Stalin shaking hands with Nazi Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop in Moscow (23 August 1939): Decades of pre-war suspicion poisoned East–West trust before 1945.
milestones.catalyst: American **free-market capitalism** and multi-party democracy clashed fundamentally with Soviet **Marxist-Leninist socialism** and one-party Communist Politburo rule.
milestones.turningPoint: Bitter memories deepened distrust: Western troops aided anti-Bolshevik Whites after **1917**, 1930s appeasement alarmed Moscow, and Stalin shocked democracies by signing the **August 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact**.
milestones.impact: Only Hitler’s 1941 invasion of Russia forced Britain, the USA, and the USSR into an uneasy wartime **Grand Alliance**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As Allied armies closed in on Nazi Germany in February 1945, the Big Three met at Yalta to bargain over post-war Europe.

keyTerms.definition: An economic system in which trade, factories, and property are owned privately for profit alongside multi-party elections.
A one-party socialist system abolishing private enterprise in favour of state-owned industry and central economic planning.
A system of core political and economic beliefs shaping how a state organises society and views rival powers.

milestones.title: The Yalta Conference: Fragile Consensus & The Polish Buffer
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did wartime allies turn into bitter rivals between Yalta and Potsdam?
milestones.imageCaption: The Big Three at Livadia Palace, Yalta (February 1945, NARA 197001): Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin agreed on four-zone Germany and the UN while clashing over Poland.
milestones.catalyst: Having suffered **27 million wartime deaths**, **Joseph Stalin** demanded a friendly Eastern European **buffer zone** so Russia could never again be invaded through Poland.
milestones.turningPoint: At **Yalta (February 1945)**, **Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin** agreed to split defeated Germany and Berlin into **four occupation zones**, found the **United Nations**, and sign the **Declaration on Liberated Europe**.
milestones.impact: Despite promising free elections, Stalin installed the communist **Lublin Poles** and sidelined democratic **London Poles**, eroding Western faith in Kremlin pledges.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Five months later at Potsdam, new Western leaders and a secret atomic breakthrough turned strained diplomacy into open confrontation.

keyTerms.definition: The wartime coalition of Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union united against Nazi Germany.
A belt of Soviet-controlled border states across Eastern Europe sought by Stalin to block future western invasions.
The right of liberated nations to choose their own governments through free, democratic elections.

milestones.title: Changing of the Guard at Potsdam & Truman’s Atomic Hint
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did wartime allies turn into bitter rivals between Yalta and Potsdam?
milestones.imageCaption: Clement Attlee, Harry S. Truman, and Joseph Stalin at Cecilienhof Palace, Potsdam (August 1945): Emboldened by the 16 July Trinity test, Truman took a tougher line with Stalin.
milestones.catalyst: Roosevelt’s death in April 1945 brought staunchly anti-communist **Harry S. Truman** to the presidency, while **Clement Attlee** replaced Churchill mid-summit after Labour’s election victory.
milestones.turningPoint: After the **16 July 1945 Trinity atomic test** in New Mexico, Truman privately told Stalin at **Potsdam** on **24 July** that America possessed *'a new weapon of unusual destructive force'*.
milestones.impact: Informed already by Soviet spies, Stalin showed calm on the surface yet read Truman’s hint as **atomic blackmail** aimed at bullying Moscow in Europe.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Days after Potsdam ended, two American atomic bombs over Japan demonstrated the terrifying reality of nuclear warfare.

keyTerms.definition: Exclusive US possession of nuclear weapons between July 1945 and the first Soviet test in August 1949.
Regions in which either the United States or the Soviet Union exercised dominant political and military control.

milestones.title: Hiroshima, Nagasaki & Launch of the Superpower Arms Race
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rival ideas turn the USA and USSR into enemies after 1945?
milestones.imageCaption: Atomic mushroom cloud rising above Hiroshima (6 August 1945): America’s nuclear monopoly prompted Stalin to order a crash Soviet atomic weapons programme.
milestones.catalyst: Seeking to force Japan’s swift surrender without a costly mainland invasion—and showcase American military power—Truman authorised combat use of the atomic bomb.
milestones.turningPoint: US bombers destroyed **Hiroshima (6 August)** and **Nagasaki (9 August 1945)**, ending the Second World War while handing Washington sole possession of atomic weapons.
milestones.impact: Refusing to bow to America’s **nuclear monopoly**, **Joseph Stalin** ordered Soviet physicists to build an atomic bomb at top speed, igniting a forty-year **nuclear arms race**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Meanwhile in defeated Germany, bitter clashes over reparations carved Europe’s heartland into separate occupation zones.

keyTerms.definition: The four-year window (1945–1949) when only the United States possessed atomic bombs.
Rival ideological systems living without direct war—strained immediately by nuclear suspicion.

milestones.title: Clashes Over $20 Billion Reparations & Four-Sector Berlin
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did wartime allies turn into bitter rivals between Yalta and Potsdam?
milestones.imageCaption: Allied commanders before the ruined Brandenburg Gate in four-sector Berlin (1945, IWM): Reparations disputes split Germany into rival eastern and western economic zones.
milestones.catalyst: Because Nazi armies had devastated western Russia, **Stalin demanded $20 billion** in German reparations, whereas **Truman and Attlee** refused to repeat Versailles’ economic collapse.
milestones.turningPoint: Under the **Allied Control Council**, each power took **reparations** mainly from its own occupation zone, leaving four-sector **Berlin** an isolated island deep inside Soviet East Germany.
milestones.impact: Meeting face to face across a ruined European power vacuum, the wartime **Grand Alliance** dissolved into rival **bipolar spheres of influence**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Early in 1946, blunt speeches in Moscow and secret cables to Washington turned quiet distrust into declared Cold War strategy.

keyTerms.definition: Post-war compensation in money, machinery, or goods taken from defeated Germany by the occupying powers.
Eastern Soviet and Western Allied zones hardening into rival political blocs across post-war Europe.

milestones.title: Stalin’s Bolshoi Speech & George Kennan’s 'Long Telegram'
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did rival ideas turn the USA and USSR into enemies after 1945?
milestones.imageCaption: Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin delivering his landmark Bolshoi Theatre election speech in Moscow (9 February 1946), answered days later by George Kennan’s Long Telegram.
milestones.catalyst: With Europe’s pre-war empires shattered, Washington and Moscow each interpreted the other’s security moves as aggressive expansion.
milestones.turningPoint: On **9 February 1946**, **Stalin** warned in Moscow that capitalism made future conflict inevitable; on **22 February**, US diplomat **George F. Kennan** sent his **8,000-word 'Long Telegram'** urging firm **containment**.
milestones.impact: Kennan’s dispatch convinced Truman’s administration that Moscow respected strength rather than concessions, forming the blueprint for forty years of US foreign policy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Weeks later in Fulton, Missouri, Winston Churchill gave a vivid name to the barrier descending across Europe.

keyTerms.definition: The US strategy proposed by George Kennan to stop Soviet communism expanding beyond its existing borders.
The industrial working class in whose name the Soviet Communist Party claimed one-party rule.

milestones.title: Churchill’s 'Iron Curtain', Truman Doctrine & $13bn Marshall Aid
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did containment and the Berlin Blockade divide Europe into rival blocs?
milestones.imageCaption: Rebuilding West Berlin with Marshall Plan aid (NARA 541691): Following Churchill’s 1946 Fulton speech and the March 1947 Truman Doctrine, the US sent over $13bn to revive Western Europe.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Stettin-to-Trieste Iron Curtain, Marshall Plan recipients, and Soviet satellite states across Europe.
milestones.catalyst: Using **'salami tactics'**—rigged elections and secret-police arrests—Moscow installed communist regimes across Eastern Europe while bankrupt Britain withdrew aid from **Greece and Turkey**.
milestones.turningPoint: After **Churchill’s March 1946 'Iron Curtain' speech** at Fulton, Truman pledged containment in the **March 1947 Truman Doctrine**, and **George Marshall** unveiled **over $13 billion** in **Marshall Plan** recovery aid (**June 1947**).
milestones.impact: Marshall Aid revived Western European industry and undermined communist appeal, while Stalin branded it **'dollar imperialism'** and barred Eastern satellites from accepting funds.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Determined to tighten Kremlin control and halt Western recovery in Germany, Stalin triggered the Cold War’s first major European crisis in 1948.

keyTerms.definition: Winston Churchill’s famous March 1946 phrase for the political and ideological barrier dividing Soviet Eastern Europe from the West.
President Truman’s March 1947 pledge of US money and military aid to help free peoples resist communist takeover.
Over $13 billion in US economic recovery funds (1948–1952) rebuilding Western Europe to prevent poverty fuelling communism.

milestones.title: Cominform, The Prague Coup & Operation Vittles Over Berlin
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did containment and the Berlin Blockade divide Europe into rival blocs?
milestones.imageCaption: Loading a USAF C-54 Skymaster during the Berlin Airlift (1948–49): Allied crews flew 2.3 million tons of coal and food into blockaded West Berlin over 324 days.
milestones.mapCaption: Cartographic map of the three 20-mile-wide Allied air corridors crossing Soviet-occupied East Germany into West Berlin.
milestones.catalyst: Following **Cominform (1947)** and the **February 1948 Prague Coup**, Britain, France, and the US merged their western German zones into **Trizonia** and launched the **Deutsche Mark** currency.
milestones.turningPoint: On **24 June 1948**, Stalin cut all road, rail, and canal links to West Berlin; led by General Lucius Clay and Ernest Bevin, the **Berlin Airlift (*Operation Vittles*)** flew in **2.3 million tons** of supplies.
milestones.impact: Refusing either to abandon West Berlin or shoot down Allied planes, **Stalin lifted the blockade after 324 days in May 1949**—a major moral victory for containment.
milestones.bridgeToNext: The Berlin crisis destroyed any remaining hope of a united Germany and locked Europe into rival military alliances.

keyTerms.definition: Stalin’s June 1948–May 1949 closure of all overland road, rail, and canal routes into Allied-held West Berlin.
The 324-day Allied aerial supply bridge ('Operation Vittles') delivering 2.3 million tons of food and fuel to West Berliners.

milestones.title: Founding of NATO & Partition into West and East Germany
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did containment and the Berlin Blockade divide Europe into rival blocs?
milestones.imageCaption: President Harry S. Truman signing the North Atlantic Treaty instrument in the Oval Office (1949, NARA 200163), binding the US and Western Europe in collective defence.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Partition of West Germany (FRG) and East Germany (GDR) alongside NATO and Warsaw Pact alliances.
milestones.catalyst: Convinced by the Prague Coup and Berlin Blockade that Western Europe needed permanent US military backing, twelve Western states met in Washington.
milestones.turningPoint: In **April 1949**, the Allies founded **NATO** pledging mutual defence, while Germany split into the democratic **Federal Republic of Germany (FRG, May 1949)** and communist **German Democratic Republic (GDR, October 1949)**.
milestones.impact: When West Germany later joined NATO in **1955**, Moscow answered with the **Warsaw Pact**, cementing two heavily armed military blocs across Europe.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even as European borders froze in late 1949, two dramatic shocks in the USSR and China turned the Cold War into a hot war in Asia.

keyTerms.definition: North Atlantic Treaty Organization (April 1949), a Western collective-defence alliance promising an attack on one is an attack on all.
An Eastern European country formally independent on paper but controlled politically and militarily by Moscow.

milestones.title: Communist China, NSC-68 & Stalemate Along Korea’s 38th Parallel
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Cold War turn into deadly wars in Korea and Vietnam?
milestones.imageCaption: US Marines landing at Inchon (15 September 1950, US DoD): After Kim Il-sung invaded South Korea, UN and Chinese armies fought to a bloody 1953 stalemate at the 38th Parallel.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Cold War Proxy Wars in Asia (1949–1975)—Communist China, Korea’s 38th Parallel DMZ, and Indochina.
milestones.catalyst: In **1949**, the **Soviet atomic test (RDS-1)** and **Mao Zedong’s** proclamation of **Communist China** prompted **NSC-68 (April 1950)** and fear of the Asian **Domino Theory**.
milestones.turningPoint: After **Kim Il-sung’s** Soviet-armed North Korean army invaded South Korea in **June 1950**, **General MacArthur’s** UN landing at **Inchon** pushed north until massive **Chinese intervention** forced a **July 1953** armistice.
milestones.impact: Korea remained divided along the **38th Parallel Demilitarized Zone** after **over three million deaths**, proving Cold War containment had become global and bloody.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In the years immediately after the Korean ceasefire, thermonuclear hydrogen bombs and covert spy agencies escalated superpower rivalry worldwide.

keyTerms.definition: A regional war in which rival superpowers arm, fund, or back opposing sides without fighting an all-out war between their homelands.
US belief that if one Asian country fell to communism, neighbouring states would topple one after another.
Fortified buffer strip along Korea’s 38th Parallel separating North and South Korea since the July 1953 armistice.

milestones.title: Castle Bravo H-Bomb & Covert CIA–KGB Shadow Operations
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why do historians argue the ‘Cold War’ was never truly cold outside Europe?
milestones.imageCaption: Mushroom cloud of America’s 15-megaton Castle Bravo hydrogen bomb test at Bikini Atoll (1 March 1954)—1,000 times more powerful than Hiroshima.
milestones.catalyst: Hydrogen bombs like **Castle Bravo (March 1954, 15 megatons)** turned open superpower war into collective suicide under **Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)**.
milestones.turningPoint: Keeping conflict below nuclear war, the **CIA** backed covert coups toppling elected governments in **Iran (*Operation Ajax*, 1953)** and **Guatemala (1954)** while the **Soviet KGB** and East German **Stasi** ran spy networks.
milestones.impact: Shadowy coups, foreign arms sales, and secret-police informers destabilised newly independent Global South nations while policing dissent behind the Iron Curtain.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Alongside covert intelligence wars on Earth, superpower competition rocketed into orbit in October 1957.

keyTerms.definition: Nuclear doctrine (MAD) in which a full-scale attack guarantees total annihilation of both superpowers.
Covert intelligence gathering, spy planes, and undercover operations waged by the CIA, KGB, and Stasi.

milestones.title: Sputnik 1, Yuri Gagarin & Ideological Rivalry in Orbit
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why do historians argue the ‘Cold War’ was never truly cold outside Europe?
milestones.imageCaption: Soviet Sputnik 1 satellite (launched 4 October 1957): Followed by Yuri Gagarin’s April 1961 orbital flight, Soviet space triumphs spurred America’s NASA Apollo Moon programme.
milestones.catalyst: Both superpowers treated rocket science as proof of which economic system—socialism or capitalism—owned the technological future.
milestones.turningPoint: Soviet engineers stunned the West by launching **Sputnik 1** (**October 1957**) and sending cosmonaut **Yuri Gagarin** into orbit (**April 1961**), spurring massive US funding for **NASA** (culminating in **Apollo 11** in 1969).
milestones.impact: Rockets capable of putting satellites in space could also hurl **ICBM nuclear warheads** across continents in minutes, intensifying strategic anxiety.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Four months after Gagarin’s flight, a refugee crisis in divided Berlin pushed East Germany and Khrushchev to seal the city in concrete.

keyTerms.definition: Intercontinental Ballistic Missile—long-range rockets developed alongside Space Race launchers to deliver nuclear warheads.
Maintaining vast nuclear missile stockpiles so neither rival dares strike first.

milestones.title: Stopping the 'Brain Drain': Construction of the Berlin Wall
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Soviet rule in Eastern Europe—and the USSR itself—collapse by 1991?
milestones.imageCaption: East German border guard stringing barbed wire in August 1961 (CIA Historical Collection): Built overnight on 13 August 1961 after 2.7 million East Germans fled west.
milestones.catalyst: Between 1949 and 1961, **over 2.7 million East Germans**—including young doctors, teachers, and engineers—escaped **Walter Ulbricht’s** harsh rule through open Berlin sectors.
milestones.turningPoint: Overnight on **13 August 1961**, Khrushchev backed Ulbricht’s troops in rolling out barbed wire and building the concrete **Berlin Wall**, followed in October by a tense US–Soviet tank standoff at **Checkpoint Charlie**.
milestones.impact: Splitting families for twenty-eight years, the Berlin Wall stabilised East Germany’s workforce yet stood worldwide—as **Kennedy** declared in 1963—as proof of communist repression.
milestones.bridgeToNext: One year after sealing Berlin, Khrushchev gambled on secretly placing nuclear missiles ninety miles off the coast of Florida.

keyTerms.definition: East Germany (GDR) and fellow Warsaw Pact regimes kept in power by Soviet backing and fortified borders.
The mass flight of 2.7 million skilled East German workers and professionals to West Berlin before August 1961.

milestones.title: Castro’s Alliance, Operation Anadyr & U-2 Discovery Over Cuba
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How close did Cuba bring nuclear war in 1962—and how was it avoided?
milestones.imageCaption: Declassified CIA U-2 reconnaissance photograph taken by Major Richard Heyser over San Cristóbal, Cuba (14 October 1962), revealing Soviet nuclear missile sites.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: San Cristóbal missile sites, Soviet nuclear strike ranges across the US, and Kennedy’s naval quarantine line.
milestones.catalyst: After **Fidel Castro’s** 1959 revolution, US trade embargoes, and Kennedy’s failed **April 1961 Bay of Pigs** exile landing, Khrushchev sought to shield Cuba and offset America’s **17-to-1 ICBM lead** and **Jupiter missiles in Turkey**.
milestones.turningPoint: Under secret **Operation Anadyr**, Moscow shipped **40,000 troops** and nuclear missiles to Cuba until **Major Richard Heyser’s U-2 spy plane** photographed launch pads at **San Cristóbal on 14 October 1962**.
milestones.impact: Briefed on 16 October, **President John F. Kennedy** convened **ExComm**, knowing Soviet missiles in Cuba could obliterate Washington and major US cities within minutes.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Over the next thirteen days, the world stood closer to thermonuclear war than at any other moment in human history.

keyTerms.definition: Pushing a dangerous superpower confrontation to the very edge of nuclear war to extract concessions.
Long-range ballistic missiles in which the United States held a 17-to-1 warhead advantage over Moscow in 1962.

milestones.title: Thirteen Days at DEFCON 2 & Vasili Arkhipov’s Veto
milestones.specTag: Enquiry 4 • Thirteen Days on the Brink
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How close did Cuba bring nuclear war in 1962—and how was it avoided?
milestones.imageCaption: US Navy P-2H Neptune patrolling above a Soviet freighter during the October 1962 Cuba quarantine while strategic bombers and missile crews stood at DEFCON 2.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The US Navy quarantine blockade ring around Cuba and Soviet convoy turn-backs in October 1962.
milestones.catalyst: ExComm generals urged immediate airstrikes and invasion of Cuba, yet **Kennedy** feared killing Soviet troops would trigger a Soviet counter-attack on **West Berlin**.
milestones.turningPoint: Kennedy ordered a naval **'quarantine'** on **22 October** at **DEFCON 2**; on **'Black Saturday' (27 October)**, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba and Soviet officer **Vasili Arkhipov** aboard submarine **B-59** refused to launch a nuclear torpedo.
milestones.impact: Arkhipov’s calm refusal under US practice depth charges—combined with Kennedy’s restraint—averted an accidental nuclear exchange at sea.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That very night of 27 October, urgent back-channel diplomacy in Washington unlocked a face-saving exit from the abyss.

keyTerms.definition: Kennedy’s selective naval blockade around Cuba, carefully named to avoid declaring formal war.
US Defense Readiness Condition—raised to DEFCON 2 (one step below nuclear war) during October 1962.

milestones.title: Secret Diplomacy, The Moscow Hotline & Partial Test Ban Treaty
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How close did Cuba bring nuclear war in 1962—and how was it avoided?
milestones.imageCaption: President John F. Kennedy in the Oval Office (October 1962): Secret back-channel talks resolved the missile crisis and led to the 1963 Hotline and Partial Test Ban Treaty.
milestones.catalyst: Both **Kennedy** and **Khrushchev** recognised that another communication delay or rogue clash could spiral instantly beyond political control.
milestones.turningPoint: Attorney General **Robert Kennedy** and Ambassador **Anatoly Dobrynin** struck a deal (**28 October 1962**): Moscow withdrew Cuban missiles for a US non-invasion pledge and secret removal of **US Jupiter missiles in Turkey**.
milestones.impact: To prevent future miscalculation, Washington and Moscow installed the **June 1963 Hotline** teletype link and signed the **August 1963 Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Stepping back from direct nuclear war after Cuba, Washington escalated military intervention half a world away in Vietnam.

keyTerms.definition: Shared recognition after October 1962 that nuclear war would destroy both superpowers completely.
Preventing superpower war through balanced retaliatory arsenals and crisis communication links like the 1963 Hotline.

milestones.title: Gulf of Tonkin Escalation & Guerrilla War in the Cu Chi Tunnels
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Cold War turn into deadly wars in Korea and Vietnam?
milestones.imageCaption: US infantry disembarking from UH-1D Huey helicopters in South Vietnam (NARA): Over 500,000 US troops fought asymmetric Vietcong guerrilla tactics and 250 km of Cu Chi tunnels.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Vietnam divided at the 17th Parallel, the Ho Chi Minh Trail, and Cu Chi tunnel operations.
milestones.catalyst: After **Ho Chi Minh** defeated France at **Dien Bien Phu (1954)** and Vietnam split at the **17th Parallel**, communist **Vietcong** guerrillas fought South Vietnam’s US-backed regime.
milestones.turningPoint: Following the **August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution**, over **500,000 US troops** waged helicopter raids with **napalm** and **Agent Orange** against fighters supplied down the **Ho Chi Minh Trail** inside **250 km of Cu Chi tunnels**.
milestones.impact: Heavy bombing and rural civilian casualties alienated Vietnamese villagers while televised bloodshed ignited mass anti-war protests across the United States.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In January 1968, a coordinated Vietcong offensive across South Vietnam shattered official US claims that victory was close.

keyTerms.definition: Irregular tactics using ambushes, booby traps, and underground tunnels to neutralise superior conventional firepower.
South Vietnamese communist guerrilla movement backed by Ho Chi Minh’s North Vietnam down the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
US strategy of trying to wear down enemy forces through body counts, air mobility, and heavy bombardment.

milestones.title: The 1968 Tet Shock, Vietnamization & The Fall of Saigon
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Cold War turn into deadly wars in Korea and Vietnam?
milestones.imageCaption: South Vietnamese evacuees aboard USS Hancock during Operation Frequent Wind as Saigon fell (April 1975, US Navy / NARA), ending America’s longest Cold War intervention.
milestones.mapCaption: Strategic theatre map of the January 1968 Tet strikes across over 100 South Vietnamese towns and cities.
milestones.catalyst: In **January 1968**, Vietcong and North Vietnamese units struck **over 100 towns** and the US Embassy in the **Tet Offensive**, stunning American television audiences.
milestones.turningPoint: **Richard Nixon** shifted to **Vietnamization** and signed the **1973 Paris Peace Accords** withdrawing US combat troops; in **April 1975**, North Vietnamese tanks captured **Saigon**.
milestones.impact: Uniting Vietnam under communist rule after **over two million deaths**, the war exposed the clear limits of superpower military might against determined nationalism.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even as diplomats celebrated European détente in 1975, historians note the Cold War stayed lethally hot across the Global South.

keyTerms.definition: Surprise lunar-new-year assault across South Vietnam that turned American public opinion decisively against the war.
Vietnam demonstrated how superpower rivalry devastated post-colonial nations even when Moscow and Washington avoided direct combat.

milestones.title: Europe’s 'Long Peace' at Helsinki vs 20 Million Global Dead
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why do historians argue the ‘Cold War’ was never truly cold outside Europe?
milestones.imageCaption: Thirty-five nations convening in Finlandia Hall for the July 1975 Helsinki Accords: While Europe kept a nuclear 'Long Peace', proxy wars killed over 20 million across the Global South.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Rival superpower alliances and Global South proxy battlegrounds across Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
milestones.catalyst: During 1970s **détente**, 35 nations signed the **July 1975 Helsinki Accords**, leading Western historians like John Lewis Gaddis to call 1945–91 Europe’s **'Long Peace'**.
milestones.turningPoint: Global historians challenge that **Eurocentric view**: while Berlin and Paris avoided war, Washington and Moscow armed dictatorships and insurgencies from **Angola** and the Middle East to **Latin America**.
milestones.impact: Across Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America, Cold War proxy conflicts killed **over twenty million people** and left millions of refugees and landmines.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In December 1979, Soviet tanks rolled into Afghanistan—shattering détente and fatally overstretching Moscow’s stagnant economy.

keyTerms.definition: The 1970s easing of direct US–Soviet tensions through summits, arms treaties, and the 1975 Helsinki Accords.
Superpower-backed conflicts across the Global South that claimed over 20 million lives between 1945 and 1991.

milestones.title: Afghan Quagmire, Reagan’s 'Star Wars' & Gorbachev’s Reforms
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Soviet rule in Eastern Europe—and the USSR itself—collapse by 1991?
milestones.imageCaption: Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev at the Geneva Summit (November 1985): Facing economic stagnation and the Afghan war, Gorbachev launched Glasnost, Perestroika, and non-intervention.
milestones.catalyst: Stagnating with food queues while spending a quarter of national wealth on arms, the USSR invaded **Afghanistan (December 1979)** against **mujahideen** fighters as **Ronald Reagan** proposed **SDI ('Star Wars')**.
milestones.turningPoint: Becoming Soviet leader in **March 1985**, **Mikhail Gorbachev** launched **Glasnost** ('openness') and **Perestroika** ('restructuring') and replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the non-interventionist **'Sinatra Doctrine'**.
milestones.impact: Once Eastern Europeans realised Red Army tanks would no longer crush reform, peaceful mass movements rose immediately to demand free elections.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Across 1989, peaceful revolutions swept from Poland and Hungary straight to the checkpoints of the Berlin Wall.

keyTerms.definition: Gorbachev’s policy of political openness, permitting freer journalism, public debate, and criticism of Soviet mistakes.
Gorbachev’s economic restructuring allowing limited private enterprise to revive the stalled Soviet command economy.

milestones.title: Breaching the Berlin Wall (1989) & Dissolution of the USSR (1991)
milestones.specTag: Enquiry 6 • End of the Cold War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Soviet rule in Eastern Europe—and the USSR itself—collapse by 1991?
milestones.imageCaption: Crowds dismantling the Berlin Wall (9–10 November 1989): Followed by German reunification in 1990 and Mikhail Gorbachev’s resignation ending the USSR on 25 December 1991.
milestones.catalyst: In 1989, Lech Wałęsa’s **Solidarity** union won free elections in Poland and Hungary opened its Austrian border, before East German spokesman **Günter Schabowski** misspoke on live TV on **9 November 1989**.
milestones.turningPoint: Jubilant Berliners breached the **Berlin Wall** (**German reunification, 1990**); after **Boris Yeltsin** defeated an **August 1991 hardline coup** in Moscow, **Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991**.
milestones.impact: As the red hammer-and-sickle flag came down over the Kremlin and **fifteen republics** gained independence, the forty-six-year Cold War ended without superpower nuclear war.
milestones.bridgeToNext: The collapse of the Soviet Union ended Europe’s forty-year division while leaving lasting geopolitical legacies across Eastern Europe and the Global South.

keyTerms.definition: Independent Polish trade union led by Lech Wałęsa whose June 1989 election victory spearheaded Eastern Europe’s peaceful revolutions.
The peaceful political and territorial union of East and West Germany in October 1990 after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
The failed August 1991 attempt by Communist hardliners to overthrow Gorbachev, hastening the breakup of the USSR.
